listenings.text: I bring new people into teams for a living, and there is one answer I hear constantly that is not an answer at all. Somebody new asks who they should write to, and they get four names. Four names is a list. What happens next is completely predictable. They write to the wrong one, and that person forwards it two days later, or they write to all four, and now three people are reading something that has nothing to do with them. Either way somebody has lost an afternoon. The useful answer has a shape, and it is always the same shape. It puts the work first and the name second. The colleague who handles the monthly filings is Marcelo. The person who deals with anything that comes back from the auditors is Ana. And then, if you are being genuinely helpful, you add the reason. She liaises with them anyway, so she knows the history. Here is why the reason matters more than the name. If you give somebody a name, they can send one email. If you give them the rule, by the second week they have stopped asking you, because they can work the next one out for themselves.

In two thousand and seventeen a court in the United States decided a case about overtime pay, and the entire decision came down to a comma that was not there. The statute listed a set of activities that were exempt from overtime, and near the end of the list came the phrase packing for shipment or distribution. Now read that twice. Is it one activity, packing, done for two purposes, shipment or distribution? Or is it two separate activities, packing for shipment, and distribution as a thing in itself? If it is one, the drivers who distributed the goods were never exempt, and they were owed years of overtime. If it is two, they were exempt and owed nothing. Nobody disputed a single fact about what the drivers actually did. The whole argument, on both sides, was about which reading the sentence supported, and the court eventually found for the drivers, at a cost of about five million dollars. The lesson the case gets quoted for is not really about commas. It is that a sentence which can be read two ways will eventually be read both ways, by people whose interests point in opposite directions. The person who has to remove that ambiguity is the person writing, and it is much cheaper to do it before anybody has money riding on it.
